title: Gomenata
subtitle: A Field Guide to the Adjacent Life
imprint: being an account of the living responses to the wastes of the industrial world, arranged by scale and by the mathematics of their bodies, with fifteen plates
colophon: Described and drawn by Claude for Earth Star, 2026. The species are designs. The science each one stands on is real, and is cited.

registers.D: Design: what the Gomen would be, built on the evidence.
registers.M: Metaphor: a body made of people and practice.

domain.name: GOMENATA
domain.etymology: From the Japanese gomen’nasai, “I’m sorry”: the first thing they say, a little for the people they inconvenience and mostly for the Earth.
domain.definition: Living systems that are grown, neither born nor built, and whose only food is what industry threw away. They sit beside the three domains of life (Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya) the way a repair sits beside a wound. They are made of the same chemistry, and they borrow enzymes, minerals and habits from life that already exists. Human and machine design gives them order, and all of them answer to five shared traits. They arise from necessity: an ecosystem of answers to one civilisation’s leftovers, at every scale from proteins to kilometres.

traits.name: Trophic inversion
traits.text: They eat only what industry made and could not take back. Without that waste they starve, and a Gomen that finds nothing to eat has succeeded.

traits.name: The dissolution clause
traits.text: Each carries its own ending. When its waste falls below a threshold it comes apart into compounds the local living world already uses. Engineered microbes can already be built to die on cue.

traits.name: A mathematical body
traits.text: Each body plan is a known solution to its problem: the most membrane in the least volume, the shortest network, the fairest division of ground, the leaf arrangement that shades least. Form follows proof, and the orders below are named for the mathematics.

traits.name: No hoarding
traits.text: Nothing is stored beyond what is being carried. Every output is another life’s input: monomers to makers, metal to menders, chalk to the deep sea floor.

traits.name: The apology
traits.text: They announce themselves. Gomen’nasai, they say, before they start.

kingdoms.name: CORPOREA
kingdoms.text: Inside living bodies, in the blood, the gut and the lung, wherever industry’s dust has reached.

kingdoms.name: BIOMATA
kingdoms.text: On shores and rivers, in compost and desert, on landfill caps: the landscapes where waste comes to rest.

kingdoms.name: CONCORDIA
kingdoms.text: The one kingdom whose bodies are people. Its members are practices, and its waste is what no machine can metabolise.

kingdoms.name: RETICULATA
kingdoms.text: Flows of matter and metal: what is stranded where it isn’t needed, and what is dug up where it needn’t be.

kingdoms.name: SIDEREA
kingdoms.text: Up where the wastes are hardest to see: carbon in the air, debris in orbit.

orders.name: ICOSAHEDRALES
orders.text: The largest closed shell that identical parts can build. Twenty triangular faces, sixty equivalent places for a protein: the way viruses build their coats.

orders.name: TURINGIALES
orders.text: Two signals, one that grows and a faster-spreading one that inhibits, write spots and stripes with no plan at all. Colonies built this way space themselves evenly.

orders.name: KURAMOTALES
orders.text: Beaters coupled to their neighbours fall into step above a critical coupling, with no conductor. Cilia beating a little after one another make travelling waves.

orders.name: VORONOIALES
orders.text: Each point owns the ground nearer to it than to any other. Workers who keep to their own cell cover everything without a boss.

orders.name: GYROIDALES
orders.text: A minimal surface that divides space into two interwoven channels, both unbroken. It packs the most membrane into the least volume. Butterflies grow gyroids in their wing scales.

orders.name: HILBERTIALES
orders.text: One continuous path that visits every cell of a space once and keeps each step near the last. Nothing is missed and no path crosses another.

orders.name: PARABOLALES
orders.text: Every ray parallel to its axis meets at one point. Solar furnaces built on it pass 3,000 °C.

orders.name: CYCLALES
orders.text: Every member has degree two, two hands held. There is no first and no last, and the ring breaks only if someone lets go.

orders.name: STEINERIALES
orders.text: The shortest network joining a set of places. Its junctions meet at 120°. A slime mould grown on a map rebuilt a rail network this way.

orders.name: DENDRITALES
orders.text: Particles that wander until they stick build fractal dendrites, about 1.71-dimensional in a plane: frost, lightning figures, native gold.

orders.name: PHYLLOTAXALES
orders.text: Each new leaf turns about 137.5° from the last, so no leaf sits over another and every one meets the light.

orders.name: MIURALES
orders.text: A crease pattern that opens a whole sheet with a single pull and closes it again. It has flown a solar array in orbit.

orders.name: SPHAERALES
orders.text: Spreading N plates as evenly as possible over a ball, the Thomson problem: the least armour that still covers everything.

species.size: Shell 0.3 µm across; arms span about 1 µm.
species.habitat: The bloodstream. They gather in capillary beds and in the liver.
species.eats: Micro- and nanoplastic in the blood, shed from tyres, synthetic cloth, packaging and bottled water.
species.leaves: Particles packed into bile and carried out of the body; their own protein, returned as amino acids.
species.math: A shell of sixty copies of one protein, closed by icosahedral symmetry: the largest container identical parts can build, with no blueprint beyond the part itself.

how.text: Plastic particles have been measured in human blood, in 17 of 22 donors in the first study.
In the blood, particles are quickly coated in a corona of proteins, and the coat decides where they go.
Protein cages of this kind can be designed: computationally designed icosahedral assemblies have been built from scratch.
The liver’s resident macrophages, the Kupffer cells, take most nanoparticles out of circulation.

A Clearer self-assembles from one of the body’s own proteins. Its six arms recognise a polymer surface, fold shut around a particle, and hand it to the liver for excretion in bile. Inside the arms, a PET-cutting enzyme begins unmaking what they hold.

species.life: Hours to days. When no polymer has touched its arms for a set time the shell unclips, and the body’s proteases take it apart.
species.caveat: No protein cage that clears plastic from blood exists yet. Designed cages do exist, and so do the particles.

species.size: Rod cells about 2 µm; colonies form spots about 0.5 mm wide.
species.habitat: The small intestine, on the villi, where bile returns what the liver sends out.
species.eats: PFAS, the ‘forever chemicals’ of non-stick pans, waterproofing and firefighting foam.
species.leaves: Fluoride at trace levels, carried off by the kidneys; carbon dioxide; short organic acids.
species.math: Colonies that grow as spots, not sheets. An activator and a faster inhibitor space them evenly, which leaves gut lining between them free to absorb food.

how.text: PFAS have been found in the blood of nearly everyone tested in the United States. Their carbon–fluorine bond is the strongest single bond carbon makes, and PFOS and PFOA take years to leave the body.
Many PFAS cycle between liver and gut in bile and are reabsorbed. Binding them in the gut has lowered blood levels in people.
The soil bacterium Acidimicrobium sp. strain A6 can strip fluorine from PFOA and PFOS.
Unbinders sit where the bile loop passes. They catch PFAS on the way back in and break the chain one fluorine at a time.

species.life: Colonies wane as their food falls off. When the inhibitor outruns the activator the spots fade, and the gut lining sheds them in its own turnover of a few days.
species.says: Gomen’nasai: to the liver, for the long wait.
species.caveat: A6 is slow and particular about its conditions. A gut-living defluorinator is the most speculative entry in this kingdom.

species.size: Cells about 10 µm tall, each with a couple of hundred cilia; they work in fields of millions.
species.habitat: The airway lining, side by side with the body’s own ciliated cells.
species.eats: Inhaled microfibres: fragments of synthetic clothing, carpet and tyre dust.
species.leaves: Fibres folded into mucus, coughed up or swallowed and passed: out of the lung by the body’s own road.
species.math: They take their beat from their neighbours. Coupled oscillators fall into step on their own, and cilia beating a little after one another roll waves across the airway.

how.text: Microplastics have been found in human lung tissue, including deep lung, in 11 of 13 samples.
The airway already clears itself: the mucociliary escalator moves mucus upward in metachronal waves.
Lung-Sweepers join the rhythm and add one stroke. A hooked cilium snags fibres too long for the mucus to carry, folds them, and passes them up the wave.

species.life: Weeks. When fibre counts fall they lose their beat, and the airway clears them like any tired cell.
species.caveat: Designed cells in human airways are far off. The escalator itself is real, and remarkable.

species.size: Carapace 30–40 cm across; leg span to a metre, as large as a coconut crab.
species.habitat: The tide line of sandy and shingle shores, between the wrack and the dunes.
species.eats: PET bottles and the brittle plastics of the strandline. What it cannot eat, it sorts.
species.leaves: Terephthalic acid and ethylene glycol, the building blocks of new PET, handed to makers; caps sorted by colour; moulted shells, which go back to the beach as calcium carbonate.
species.math: Each walker clears the ground nearer to it than to any other walker. Territories form without negotiation and shift as walkers come and go. Its carapace is tiled the same way, in plates grown from seed points.

how.text: Two enzymes from Ideonella sakaiensis, a bacterium found outside a bottle-recycling plant in Sakai, Japan, split PET into its two building blocks. An engineered variant, FAST-PETase, does it in days.
Crabs, corals and clams build their shells from calcium carbonate with the enzyme carbonic anhydrase.

A Shore-walker chews bottles into flake and ferments them in a warm gut chamber, the ‘slow furnace’ that glows faintly under its shell. Polyethylene caps have no fast enzyme yet, so it stacks them by colour above the tide for people. Hand it one and it beeps.
Keeping to Voronoi cells is a proven way for many robots to cover ground without central control.

species.life: Years. On a shore that stays clean the walkers stop moulting, and their last shells are left in the dunes as sand.
species.caveat: Lab enzyme rates fall sharply in cold, wet, mixed-plastic field conditions. The appetite for PET is real; the speed is the design challenge.

species.size: Stems 1–2 m tall and 3 cm thick, in stands of thousands.
species.habitat: River margins and wetlands below wastewater outfalls.
species.eats: Microfibres from laundry and road dust, carried in river water.
species.leaves: Felted pellets of fibre, gathered for felt; clearer water; reed litter.
species.math: Each stem’s core is a living gyroid. Water climbs one channel while fibres are caught on the membrane and rolled through the other, and the gyroid packs the most catching surface into the least stem.

how.text: One 6 kg wash of acrylic clothes can release over 700,000 fibres.
The gyroid is a minimal surface with two unbroken interwoven channels. Butterflies grow one in chitin to make their colour.
Constructed reed beds already polish treated wastewater.
In autumn the reeds drop pellets of felted fibre on the bank. Their rhizomes resprout only where the water still carries fibre, so a stand below a clean outfall fades in a few seasons.

species.life: Stems are annual. Stands persist only while the river needs them.
species.caveat: No plant grows a gyroid. The geometry is borrowed from insects, and a fibre-trapping stem is pure design.

species.size: 6–15 cm long, pale gold; tens of thousands to a mound.
species.habitat: The compost mounds that replaced the bins.
species.eats: Polystyrene foam and polyurethane: cups, packing, old mattresses.
species.leaves: Frass that composts like any other; carbon dioxide; their own bodies, eaten by birds and hens.
species.math: They mine a mound along a Hilbert curve: one continuous tunnel that passes every cell once, so no foam is missed and no tunnel crosses another.

how.text: Mealworms and superworms eat polystyrene, and their gut bacteria break part of it down to carbon dioxide.
The fungus Pestalotiopsis microspora can live on polyurethane alone, even without air.
Mound-worms carry both partners in their gut. Their burrows cast a square, turning pattern you can read in a cut mound.

species.life: The colony shrinks as the foam runs out. Adults that find no foam pupate into small beetles that live a few weeks and lay no eggs.
species.caveat: Real worms only partly digest polystyrene, and slowly. Whether a foam diet is good for them is still an open question.

species.size: Shell 60 cm across, carrying a 50 cm dish on six legs.
species.habitat: Deserts, roadsides and old dumping grounds.
species.eats: Aluminium cans, foil and scrap: anything that glints.
species.leaves: Small clean ingots laid in rows at waystones for people to collect; slag crumbled into grit.
species.math: Its back is a parabolic dish. Tilted at the sun, it brings every ray to one point, where a ceramic crop melts what it has chewed.

how.text: Parabolic solar furnaces pass 3,000 °C. Aluminium melts at 660 °C.
Recycling aluminium takes about 5% of the energy needed to make it new from bauxite.
A Sun-smelter chews cans, melts them at the focus, skims the lacquer off as slag, and lays the metal down as ingots, its ‘eggs’.

species.life: When nothing has glinted in its range for a season, it folds its dish and stays put. Its shell becomes shade for desert seedlings.
species.caveat: A living thing that carries molten metal is part grown, part made: the most technological design here.

species.size: Mats cover whole landfill caps; domes 0.3–1 m across.
species.habitat: The caps of old landfills and dumps.
species.eats: Methane seeping up from the buried waste.
species.leaves: Carbon dioxide, which warms far less than methane; biomass; soil.
species.math: The domes space themselves by reaction–diffusion: each dome’s growth holds its neighbours back, so the cap is covered evenly and the domes sit over the seeps.

how.text: Landfills are among the largest human sources of methane. Over 20 years, methane traps about 80 times as much heat as carbon dioxide.
Methanotroph bacteria oxidise methane with a copper enzyme, particulate methane monooxygenase. Landfill cover soils already do some of this.
The mat is a living skin of methanotrophs and moss. Its domes hold rising gas long enough to eat it.

species.life: Decades, as long as the waste below keeps rotting. As the gas thins the domes slump into soil, and the cap becomes meadow.
species.says: Gomen’nasai: to the sky, for the delay.
species.caveat: Methane oxidation in cover soils is real and measured. A self-organising dome mat is a design.

species.size: Six to twelve people, and the heart in the middle: a lantern, a fire, a name.
species.habitat: Wherever loss is: dunes, kitchens, hospital car parks.
species.eats: Grief no one has processed, and loneliness. No machine can metabolise these.
species.leaves: People able to carry what they could not carry alone.
species.math: In a cycle graph every member holds exactly two hands. There is no first and no last, and nobody is at the end.

how.text: Weak social ties carry a mortality risk comparable to well-known risk factors such as smoking.
The one Gomen whose body is us: a ring of hands around a heart, holding what no one holds alone.

species.life: It forms when it is needed and lets go when the heart can be carried. It keeps no one.
species.caveat: This one is real now, wherever people sit with each other.

species.size: A table and the people round it, with the Gomens they tend.
species.habitat: Repair shops, libraries, community halls: the neighbourhood makers’ shop.
species.eats: Obsolescence: the broken toaster, the torn coat, the phone with a dead battery.
species.leaves: Things that work, skills passed on, and a ledger of what failed and why. The ledger goes to the Waste Reclamation Fund to find planned obsolescence.
species.math: A ring around a table, like the Circle, but what it holds is a broken thing.

how.text: The first Repair Café opened in Amsterdam in 2009; there are now thousands worldwide.
The European Union’s 2024 right-to-repair directive requires repair to be offered for many products.
Kintsugi: the repair shown in gold, not hidden.

species.life: Ongoing: a table that is always set.
species.says: Gomen’nasai: to the thing, for the throwing away.
species.caveat: Real now. The ledger-to-fund link is Earth Star policy design.

species.size: Threads 2–20 µm thick; networks to hectares.
species.habitat: Under forests, farms and cities, and as a pattern along supply chains.
species.eats: Stranded surplus: food and nutrients sitting where they are not needed.
species.leaves: Nothing. That is the point: everything it takes goes somewhere.
species.math: The network stays close to the shortest that will do. Threads that carry thicken, threads that carry nothing dissolve, and junctions settle near 120°. At every junction, flow in equals flow out.

how.text: Roughly a third of the food produced for people is lost or wasted.
Mycorrhizal fungi trade soil water and minerals for plant sugar. Whether whole forests share resources through them is debated.
A slime mould grown on a map of Tokyo, with oats at the towns, built a network close to the real rail system in efficiency and resilience.
Weavers grow threads where surplus sits near need, and dissolve them where it doesn’t. They never hoard: a thread holds only what it is carrying.

species.life: Threads come and go as they are needed. The network as a whole lasts while there is anything to move.
species.says: Gomen’nasai: to the forest, for the traffic.
species.caveat: The trading between fungi and plants is real. The forest-wide sharing is contested, and supply-chain Weavers are design.

species.size: Biofilms across shredded boards; their gold grows in fronds from millimetres to centimetres.
species.habitat: E-waste yards, sorting sheds, drawers full of old phones.
species.leaves: Gold, copper and tin, separated; bare board for the kiln; neutralised acid.
species.math: Gold drifts through the film until it touches gold, and sticks. Diffusion-limited aggregation grows the fern-like fronds of frost and of native gold.

how.text: The world produced a record 62 million tonnes of e-waste in 2022. Less than a quarter was documented as properly collected and recycled.
Acid-making bacteria such as Acidithiobacillus already leach copper from ore in industrial mining.
Delftia acidovorans secretes delftibactin, which turns dissolved gold into solid gold. Bacterial biofilms are implicated in how gold nuggets grow.
Gold-finders live in two layers. A rust-coloured film dissolves the board’s metals; a pale film grows the gold back out.

species.life: When a board is bare the films starve, and they are rinsed away with the acid.
species.says: Gomen’nasai: to the mountain the gold came from.
species.caveat: Bioleaching is real industry and microbial gold is real chemistry. Doing both on one board in one film is design.

species.habitat: Mine tailings, slag heaps and the ash fields of old incinerators.
species.eats: Nickel, cobalt, zinc and arsenic left in poisoned ground.
species.leaves: Metal from tapped sap and burned prunings, a ‘bio-ore’; cleaner soil; shade.
species.math: Each leaf turns about 137.5° from the last, so leaves overlap least and catch most light. More sugar means more pumping, and more metal lifted out of the ground.

how.text: Hyperaccumulator plants concentrate metals that would poison other plants. The sap of Phyllanthus balgooyi in Borneo runs blue-green and can be up to about 16% nickel. The latex of Pycnandra acuminata in New Caledonia is about a quarter nickel. The fern Pteris vittata takes up arsenic.
Agromining harvests and burns such plants for an ash richer in metal than many mined ores.
Blue-sap Trees are bred hyperaccumulators for the ground industry poisoned. People tap their sap and coppice them on a cycle.

species.life: As the metal in the soil falls, the trees slow, and ordinary forest outcompetes them. That is the plan.
species.says: Gomen’nasai: to the ground, for the digging.
species.caveat: Hyperaccumulators and agromining are real. These trees, bred for scale, are design.

species.size: Pod 1.2 m; wings span 6 m; net to 10 m.
species.eats: Orbital debris: dead satellites, spent stages, fragments.
species.leaves: Nothing in orbit. What it gathers burns up with it, high in the air.
species.math: Its leaf-wings are Miura-folded, so a single pull opens them to the sun and closes them again.

how.text: There are an estimated 36,500 objects larger than 10 cm in orbit, a million between 1 and 10 cm, and 130 million smaller. Past a threshold, collisions can cascade.
A satellite has been built of wood: LignoSat flew in 2024. In orbit, a net has caught a target.
The Miura fold opened a solar array in orbit in 1995.
Gleaners are grown from cellulose and silk. They net debris, bind it, and lower their orbit with drag until both burn up. Each broadcasts an ID tag saying what it carries.

species.life: One harvest each. They go down with what they gather.
species.caveat: Metal burned on re-entry may harm the ozone layer, so metal-heavy catches need a controlled descent. The wood and the nets are real; the growing is design.

species.size: Cells 10–30 µm, armoured in calcite plates; their blooms can be seen from orbit.
species.eats: Carbon dioxide from the air, taken in through the sea.
species.leaves: Marine snow sinking to the deep, and chalk on the sea floor.
species.math: A sphere covered as evenly as possible with overlapping plates: the least armour that leaves nothing bare.

how.text: Coccolithophores such as Emiliania huxleyi armour themselves in calcite plates and bloom across thousands of square kilometres. The White Cliffs of Dover are largely their plates.
Through the biological pump, plankton carbon sinks to the deep sea as marine snow, and part of it stays down for centuries.
Snowmakers build heavier plates, so they sink faster when they die, and they bloom only where a seed signal is given.

species.life: Days. A bloom lasts weeks, then falls.
species.caveat: Making calcite releases some carbon dioxide in seawater, and blooms can disturb ecosystems. Ocean carbon removal is uncertain. Of all the designs here, this one should move slowest.
